text:
The city, known as Zephyria, was not merely built upon the sands but seemed to have been exhaled by the desert itself. Its architecture, a testament to centuries of adaptation, featured towering domes crafted from pale, heat-reflecting limestone that shimmered with an iridescent sheen under the midday sun. These domes, interconnected by intricate arches and covered walkways, created a labyrinthine network of shade and light, allowing the city to breathe in the cool evening air while shielding its inhabitants from the relentless daytime heat.

Historically, Zephyria emerged during the Age of Caravans, a period when the great trade routes connecting the eastern spice lands to the western maritime empires converged at this oasis. It became a melting pot of cultures, where merchants from the Jade Kingdoms, the Iron Steppes, and the Southern Isles exchanged not only goods but also stories, languages, and traditions. The marketplace, the heart of the city, was a sensory overload of scents—spices, leather, and exotic fruits—mixed with the cacophony of haggling voices in a dozen different tongues.

In this vibrant hub, the most common yellow fruit that monkeys also eat is the banana. These fruits, imported from the lush southern jungles via the same caravan routes, were a staple in the market, prized for their sweetness and nutritional value, and often traded alongside silk and gold.
